title: Islamic Golden Age
license: CC BY-SA 4.0; see source history and contributors
text:
The Islamic Golden Age was a period of cultural flourishing in the history of Islam, dated from the 8th century CE to the 14th century. The period is understood to have begun during the reign of the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid (786–809), with the establishment of the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, one of the world's largest cities at the time. The institution attracted scholars from across the Muslim world to translate the classical knowledge of the known world into Arabic. Cairo also served as a major intellectual center for the Islamic world, notably through the founding of the House of Knowledge and Al-Azhar University, one of the world's oldest universities.
In addition to Baghdad, and Cairo, the intellectual and cultural activity also flourished in other urban centers of the medieval Islamic world, including Umayyad Córdoba (capital of Al-Andalus), as well as Damascus, Nishapur, Samarkand, Ghazni, Kairouan, and Fez, and in later centuries, Nasrid Granada.
The period is said to have ended with the collapse of the Abbasid caliphate following the Mongol invasions and the Siege of Baghdad in 1258. Select scholars extend the end of the golden age to around 1350, thereby including the Timurid Renaissance. Other scholars extend it to the 15th century, including the Nasrid Kingdom of Granada, whose court remained an important centre of scholarship, culture and literature, or even to the 17th century, incorporating the rise of the Islamic gunpowder empires.
